2  Obtaining performance from a third party: ‘replacement’
Civil Code
Art. 1222.—​Having given notice to perform, a creditor may also himself, within 
a reasonable time and at a reasonable cost, have an obligation performed or, 
with the prior authorisation of the court, may have something which has been 
done in breach of an obligation destroyed. He may claim reimbursement of 
sums of money employed for this purpose from the debtor.
He may also bring proceedings in order to require the debtor to advance a sum 
necessary for this performance or destruction.
In the remedy of replacement (faculté de remplacement), the defaulting party is re­
quired to indemnify the injured party in respect of the cost of employing a third 
party to perform the obligation that has been breached. It is hybrid in nature, in 
that it has characteristics of specific enforcement and compensatory damages. The 
injured party obtains an equivalent of the promised performance but the defaulting 
party is liable only to pay a monetary sum.90
Before the reforms, there was a debate as to the true nature of replacement. 
It was thought by some commentators to be closer to specific enforcement than 
damages.91 This has now implicitly been confirmed by article 122292 being posi­
tioned in the section of the new Civil Code on enforced performance in kind 
(exécution forcée en nature), immediately after article 1221, which establishes the 
centrality of specific enforcement. That said, from a common law perspective, it 
more closely resembles compensatory damages93 in that the injured party obtains 
substitute performance as if an award of damages on the cost of cure basis has 
been made.
